example: Ask "What was the best part of your day?" and listen to the full answer.
Ask "What made you laugh today?"
Ask about their favourite game or YouTube channel and listen to the full answer.
Share a short story about your own day, so they learn to share theirs too.
Ask "Is there anything on your mind?" and just listen.
Give a hug when you say goodbye and again when you meet up.
Say "I love you", face to face.
Give a high-five or fist bump after a good effort.
Leave a small sticky note with a smiley where your child will find it.
Ruffle their hair or give a gentle shoulder squeeze as you walk past.
"You packed your school bag by yourself. That was really responsible."
"I noticed you shared your snack with your brother. That was kind."
"You kept trying that maths problem even when it was hard. I'm proud of your effort."
"Thank you for setting the table without being asked."
"You stayed calm even though you were upset. That took self-control."
Put down your phone and make eye contact when your child starts talking.
Pause what you're doing for one minute when they say "Look at this!"
Watch them show off a skill, such as a skipping trick or a drawing, and react with interest.
Ask follow-up questions about what they just told you.
Notice small things, such as "You got a new haircut!" or "You seem tired today."
Share a meal together with all phones put away.
Play one round of a board or card game together.
Take a 15-minute walk around the neighbourhood together.
Let your child pick a show and watch it together, snuggled on the sofa.
Do a short "just us two" outing, such as getting ice cream at the void deck or nearby shop.
Bake cookies or a simple cake together.
Do a mini science experiment at home, such as a baking soda volcano.
Build a LEGO set or a cardboard fort together.
Go on a nature trail or cycling trip at a park.
Have a family craft session, such as painting or making DIY (Do-It-Yourself) cards.
Say "sorry" to your child when you make a mistake.
Let them see you read a book instead of scrolling your phone.
Tidy up after yourself, and let them see you do it.
Say "please" and "thank you" to the family, shop staff and delivery riders.
Stay calm and talk it through when you disagree with someone, so they see how to handle conflict.
At the supermarket, let your child compare prices and pick the better deal (maths and money skills).
While cooking, let them measure ingredients (fractions).
On an MRT (Mass Rapid Transit) ride, ask them to read the route map and find the next interchange.
While walking, point out a plant, insect or bird and wonder aloud about it together.
While watching the news, ask "How do you think that person feels?" (empathy).
Ask: "Can you help me clear the table?" Say: "Plates go to the sink." Do: carry the dishes together.
Ask: "Shall we tidy your room?" Say: "Toys go in the box, books on the shelf." Do: sort one section together first.
Ask: "Can you pack your bag for tomorrow?" Say: "Check your timetable." Do: go through the list side by side the first time.
Ask: "Want to learn to fold laundry?" Say: "Fold it in half, then in thirds." Do: demonstrate with one shirt.
Ask: "Can you help water the plants?" Say: "Just enough to wet the soil." Do: water one pot together, then let them try.
Ask your child to teach you something they learned this week, and ask a follow-up question.
Tell your child about something you were proud of when you were their age.
Pick a song together and each say what it reminds you of.
Share one small thing that was tricky for you today and what you did about it.
Play three rounds of "would you rather" with silly choices.
Take turns drawing each other in 60 seconds, with no judging.
Build a three-sentence story together, one sentence each.
Give a long hug and count to ten before letting go.
Hold their hand while you walk together, even for a short stretch.
Invent a secret handshake or special wave that's just for the two of you.
Give a thumbs-up and a big smile across the room when they catch your eye.
Offer a gentle back rub or head scratch while they relax.
"You kept your voice down while your sister was resting. That was thoughtful."
"You helped your friend work it out instead of just giving the answer. That was patient."
"I saw you put your shoes neatly on the rack. Thank you for taking care of our home."
"You tried a new food even though you weren't sure. That was brave."
"You said sorry and meant it. That takes courage."
Stop what you're doing and turn your whole body towards them when they speak.
Crouch or sit at their eye level when they want to show you something.
Say back what they told you in your own words ("So you felt left out when...") to show you were listening.
Look closely at their drawing, homework or toy and name one detail you like.
Let them finish their whole story without interrupting, even if it wanders.
At the hawker centre, let them read the menu board and work out the total cost of your order (maths and money skills).
When you see a long word on a sign, ask them to sound it out and guess what it means (reading).
At a pedestrian crossing, ask them why we wait for the green man (safety and rules).
When something breaks at home, ask them to guess the cause and what to try first (problem solving).
When you look at the sky together, ask what shape a cloud looks like and what it might do next (curiosity).
Ask: "Can you help me wipe the table?" Say: "Wipe one way, then the other way." Do: wipe one half together, then let them do the rest.
Ask: "Want to help sort the recycling?" Say: "Clean paper, plastic bottles and cans go in the blue bin." Do: sort the first few items together.
Ask: "Can you help me pack your sports bag?" Say: "Tick off each item on the list." Do: pack the first item together.
Ask: "Shall we make your bed together?" Say: "Pull the sheet flat, then the blanket." Do: fix one side together, then let them do the other.
Ask: "Can you help carry the groceries?" Say: "Hold the bag with both hands." Do: carry one bag side by side.
